title: Elephant Rescued After Fall at Milwaukee County Zoo - NewsBreak
text:
By Lil Zim ,
2 hours ago
Emergency crews were called to Milwaukee County Zoo this week, but not for a visitor or staff member who needed help. They were called to help an old elephant get back on its feet.
ArtShotPhoto Favorite Zoos in Wisconsin My kids are HUGE animal lovers, so going to a zoo is something my family does at least once a year.
Living in Northern Illinois, we are pretty lucky to have some amazing zoos like Brookfield Zoo , Lincoln Park Zoo , or even Summerfield Zoo in Belvidere just a short drive from home, and trust me, my family has been to all of them. Multiple times.
In just a few weeks my family is planning to head to Wisconsin , and a stop at Milwaukee County Zoo is already on the to-do list. Let’s hope our upcoming visit will be far less eventful than what other zoo visitors witnessed on Tuesday, September 2.
Elephant Emergency at Milwaukee County Zoo On Tuesday morning Ruth, one of Milwaukee County Zoo’s African savanna elephants, tripped and fell over a log after she was nudged by another elephant. Obviously, falling down is never good, but when you’re a 43-year-old “geriatric” elephant with arthritis, falling down can cause serious health issues. Thankfully she had some quick-thinking and compassionate zoo keepers and emergency personnel who jumped into action.
After discovering Ruth was unable to get up on her own, zoo staff “ called the Milwaukee Fire Department Heavy Urban Rescue Team and Dawes Rigging and Crane, who remained on standby ” according to WISN , but it turns out all that was needed was a front loader and some hay bales to save the day:
After getting a gentle nudge back on her feet, Ruth walked right into her enclosure and was immediately checked over by zoo medical staff who thankfully, gave her a good bill of health.

WOW: 19 Exotic-Looking Animals Surprisingly Found in America While some are native and others arrived by accident, there are animals living quite happily in the U.S. that will make you say, “No way!” From seriously big cats to the pinkest bird you’ve ever seen, here are some of the most exotic creatures calling America home. Gallery Credit: Stephen Lenz Getty Images The Roseate Spoonbill Not subtle in the least, the bubble-gum hued weird cross between a spoon and a flamingo easily stands out among the marshes of Florida, Texas, and Louisiana. Once endangered thanks to being prized for their gorgeous feathers, the spoonbill has made a nice comeback and has even made some unexpected appearances in places where it really stands out , like Maine and Minnesota. Getty Images Seneca White Deer You might think you are seeing ghosts, but these elusive, all-white deer roam the former Seneca Army Depot . Since they are in a protected area, the recessive leucistic gene survives, making them the largest herd of white deer in the world. Getty Images Wild Horses of Assateague Island Sometimes called the "Chincoteague ponies," these stunning free-roaming animals are descended from domestic horses that made the island their home . You might think they are all pregnant or perhaps a little over-indulgent, but their bloated bellies are actually a symptom of their salty diet, seeing that they live so close to the ocean. Getty Images The Parrots of Telegraph Hill, San Francisco They aren't the only non-native parrot population in the U.S., but they might be the most famous. Starring in the popular 2007 documentary The Parrots of Telegraph Hill , the red-capped parrots in San Francisco (actually cherry-headed conures) are known for their loud squeaking, playful antics, and big personalities.
The brightly colored birds are descended from escaped pets and now number in the hundreds. Getty Images The Wild Burros of Arizona You may only expect to see donkeys causing a ruckus at the local barnyard, but Oatman, Arizona's wild burros have made quite a name for themselves.
Roaming freely, these descendants of 19th-century mining pack animals have adapted quite nicely to the area's desert conditions, but as is often the case, growing numbers have raised concerns about their impact on the local ecology. Getty Images The Javelina It might scream pig, but it's a peccary , and it makes its home with 20 family members at a time in Arizona. They like prickly pears and are known to invade backyards looking for tasty veggie treats. Getty Images The Wolverine Found from Montana and Idaho to Washington and Oregon, these fierce creatures are built like tanks, with paws that seem way too big for their bodies.
The wolverine is one of those animals that makes people say, “Wait, that’s real?” It is—and it’s spectacularly elusive, often earning nicknames like “ghost of the forest” or “phantom of the Rockies.” Getty Images The Monkeys of Silver Springs State Park, Florida The U.S. doesn’t have any native primates—but don’t tell that to the rowdy rhesus macaques living their best lives in sunny Florida. Descended from a colony introduced as part of a jungle cruise attraction, these wild monkeys now number in the hundreds.
It’s not all monkey business, though—there’s ongoing concern that their growing population could contribute to the spread of diseases like herpes B . Getty Images The Hellbender It might be scientifically known as America's largest salamander, but it's more lovingly known as the "snot otter" or "lasagna lizard." While the name screams terror, it's a gentle giant and spends time lounging in rivers from New York to Missouri and breathing through skin folds, because why not?
And while it might be hard to tell by the photo, these beasts can grow fro 12 - 20 inches and weigh up to 5 pounds. Getty Images The Coatimundi (or Coati) The coatimundi (or coati) looks part raccoon and part… we aren't quite sure. With its long snout and agile tree-climbing skills, this odd-looking creature is a cousin of America’s favorite dumpster panda, the raccoon.
Coatis are native to the American Southwest, including Arizona, which is seemingly a hotbed for weird animals. Getty Images The Lined Seahorse It seems like every few years, there's another story about a surprising animal living in New York City's Hudson River, from humpback whales to manatees , but that also includes one that we only expect to see in tropical waters and fancy aquariums — the seahorse .
The lined seahorse lives quite happily in brackish waters (where salt and fresh water meet) in NYC's Hudson River. Getty Images The Oryx A stunning specimen of an antelope, you’d probably crash your car into a light pole if you saw an oryx roaming along the highway — but these desert dwellers, native to Africa and the Middle East, have also been introduced to southern New Mexico, where the arid climate suits them just fine.
About 95 of these animals were introduced to the White Sands Missile Range and surrounding areas between 1969 and 1977. Getty Images The American Pika See a picture of one of these cuties and you can almost hear Richard Attenborough narrating the pika's furry antics in the highest reaches of the Andes. But these hamster-sized fluffballs are actually living it up on the slopes of the Rocky Mountains and other western alpine regions.
They’re best known for frantically spending their summers building “haypiles” to eat during brutal winters — not too different from the average squirrel or chipmunk living under your front porch. Getty Images The Gila Monster Not to be outdone in the scary name department by the hellbender, the Gila monster is a venomous, sluggish lizard found in the deserts of (again!) Arizona, New Mexico, Nevada, and parts of California.
While the same can’t be said for small rodents (see photo), the Gila monster rarely poses a threat to humans. Surprisingly, its venom has played a role in the development of medications for type 2 diabetes. Getty Images The Ringtail While easily mistaken for a cat, an escaped lemur, or maybe some adorable creature dreamed up by PIXAR, the ringtail is actually a nocturnal relative of the raccoon found across the southwestern U.S. This little acrobat with big eyes (perfect for night vision) is elusive and rarely seen in urban areas—but when it is, it's a delightful surprise. Getty Images The Jaguar Probably the most surprising member of this list, jaguars still roam parts of the U.S. today , though sightings are extremely rare. When they are spotted, it’s usually in the rugged mountains of southern Arizona and New Mexico.
Most recently, male jaguars like the one affectionately known as " El Jefe " have been tracked crossing from Mexico, giving fans of the elusive big cat hope for a comeback. Getty Images Tardigrades (or Water Bears) While they may be microscopic, tardigrades are extreme — they can live anywhere from a patch of grass in your backyard to the deepest ocean trenches, and even outer space. These eight-legged creatures have survived boiling, freezing, and radiation exposure.
All that, and there are probably a couple thousand within 20 feet of you right now.
